newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Ministers head into late-night tussle over fish quotas.
newsitem.headline: Ministers head into late-night tussle over fish quotas.

text.p: European Union fisheries ministers began haggling on Thursday over 1997 fish catch quotas after agreeing a satellite fisheries control system and delaying a decision over fleet cuts.
Ireland, presiding over the last ministerial meeting of its EU presidency which ends on December 31, was drawing up a compromise proposal after bilateral talks with member states.

It will try to balance the proposal of the European Commission, which is seeking modest cuts to protect fish stocks, with demands from ministers, under strong pressure from fishermen, for higher quotas.
"The compromise will try to reconcile conservation and economic needs," an Irish official said, noting that ministers had moved swiftly through a long list of non-quota issues.
Ministers earlier agreed to set up a satellite system from mid-1998 to survey movements of fishing vessels over a length of 24 metres in a bid to curb illegal fishing.
Smaller vessels fishing for less than 24 hours and within 12 miles of the coast will be exempted from the EU-funded scheme.
"(It's) a very strategic and significant tool in the ongoing battle against illegal fishing," Sean Barrett, Irish marine minister, said in a statement.
But ministers postponed until next April a decision on controversial plans for sharp cuts in fishing fleets over the next six years to protect dwindling fish stocks.
EU aid for fishermen laying up vessels and leaving the industry will be stopped when the current five-year programme expires at the end of 1996.
But fishermen will be able to claim aid retroactively provided a new programme is agreed by April 30, 1997, Commission officials said.

EU officials said one of the main scraps on quotas will be over fishing in the Baltic for cod, herring and salmon now that Sweden and Finland's membership of the EU has ended their bilateral accords with Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania.
Germany, Denmark and Finland strongly oppose the proposed re-allocation of fishing rights.

Another potential flashpoint is over measures to halt the decline of sardine stocks off Spain and Portugal while Italy and Greece will be fighting over new quotas for bluefin tuna in the Mediterranean and Atlantic and for swordfish in the Atlantic.

The Commission also wants to slash North Sea sole catches by half to 12,000 tonnes because stocks are at critical levels. The reduction, which would also affect fishing for plaice, would affect mainly British and Dutch fishermen.
Emergency measures taken in July to protect critically low herring stocks and fixing a 1997 total allowable catch (TAC) of 159,000 tonnes, half the 1995 level, would be extended.
The new quotas are based on international scientific advice.
